abstract: Root-knot nematodes (RKNs) are a major concern for tomato growers worldwide. Management relies heavily on the plant resistance gene Mi-1, which has been bred into most processing tomato cultivars. However, repeated use of Mi-1 has placed strong selection pressure on nematode populations, promoting the emergence of resistance-breaking isolates. Despite the growing impact of resistance-breaking RKNs, their frequency, distribution, and species identity across California remain poorly understood. In this study, we isolated RKN isolates from processing tomato fields at 14 sites across California, identified them to species, and evaluated their reproduction on current rotation crops to determine whether crop rotation could suppress these populations. All 14 sites yielded resistance-breaking populations, and most isolates were M. incognita. A SNP-based principal component analysis revealed substantial genetic diversity among several isolates, suggesting that resistance-breaking emerged independently in multiple fields rather than all spreading from a single population. In greenhouse assays, alfalfa displayed the lowest reproduction of both wild-type and resistance-breaking M. incognita, whereas reproduction on other rotation crops varied by isolate. Together, these results show that rotation decisions should be guided by local RKN population identity and host compatibility rather than generalized strategies across fields.
